content:
@Shreyas Srinivas @Kim Morrison thanks for all the work into those PRs. I have plenty of comments, but to optimise everybody's time I'd like to understand better how TimeM, cslib#372, and cslib#376 compare. Let's focus on key points.

In a nutshell, cslib#372 gives us signatures like

def insertionSort (l : List α) : Prog (SortOpsInsertHead α) (List α)

which fights cheating through interpretation (FreeM/Prog).

By contrast, cslib#376 gives us:

public def insertionSort [Monad m] (cmp : α × α → m Bool) : List α → m (List α)

which fights cheating through parametric polymorphism.

I have two questions:

  1. After squinting my eyes for a while, I could imagine ways to do almost anything interesting in both approach (reusing the same algorithm with different cost models, doing parametric complexity, proving lower bounds, etc.). Is that actually true?
  2. Real bliss in this case would be using a typeclass instead of an explicit parameter for the operations, for example:
public def insertionSort [Monad m] [LE α] : List α → m (List α)

Can that be done?
Please note cslib#275 is closed in favor of cslib#372. They are the same with squashed commit history that made it easier to review.
That's the one I meant, thanks for spotting it. Edited.

the point with cslib#372 is beyond just getting rid of cheating. In terms of “cheat”ability both PRs are close (and substantially better than TimeM) but as @Eric Wieser pointed out, passing explicit comparison functions can cause problems. I will let him address that issue
The point of my Prog approach is to go far beyond what TimeM and TickM can
To allow explicit reasoning about model and reductions between them
And about lower bounds in some cases
As I showed in an earlier thread we can also handle circuits (which means we can handle parallel algorithms)
To be clear, what you're claiming is that all of that cannot be done in cslib#376?
Yes
And there’s more

With an explicit query model approach we can

  1. Have multiple cost models for the same query (you see examples in one of my test files)
  2. You can pursue a top down and modular approach to algorithms formalization.

To elaborate on 2. What I mean is that we follow algorithms papers and encode their opaque subroutines from Literature as queries. Then we reduce those custom queries to more basic queries, all the way down to standard models
So we have clear reduction theorems
I can also use this framework to make working with explicit TMs quite a bit simpler
And since both circuits and TMs can fit into the same web of reductions, we have a chance to finally tackle uniform circuits

slightly different issue

The generalisations of CSLib#376 could (and ideally should) be built on top of cslib#372 by converting Prog from a free monad to a free monad transformer.
For algorithms theory I’d not use this hypothetical ProgT with any monad other than Id because adding extra monads has unexplored questions of soundness w.r.t complexity models.

And to also be clear. None of the models above completely disallow “cheating”. They just reduce it to a point where a reviewer can easily spot it. As soon as you have a query (on in the case of cslib#376 ‘s case a function) that performs what I call a “write-operation” it can be substituted by a pure operation.

This is an inherent limitation of any monadic lightweight approach which will require human review to avoid. Both these approaches simplify this review process over TimeM. But with CSLib#372 as Eric can explain, this is simpler because of the upfront statement of queries and costs.

And I claim that we actually want this explicit commitment for all the reasons above. In general if one cannot commit to a cost model and operations to count in advance, it is much more dangerous to do this inside an algorithm.
An interesting aspect of 376 is its usage of mvcgen. It would be nice to make use of this, so I'd like to understand if its possible and/or what this would look like with the free monad approach.
Yes
I haven’t done this because my pr is big enough as it is
But I think the basic approach of cslib#376 can be ported to cslib#372 (in a future PR)
After all we are just evaluating in the Id monad
And Fabrizio : I think the extra annotation’s flexibility is important.

Today you might have an opaque query for computation Z with one cost model. Tomorrow there might be a better algorithm for Z with better time complexity. You might just want to give your existing query a new cost model for Z.
(note that I have some thoughts here but am away on vacation for the next week and a bit so may not find time to collect them)

There might be two ways of building cslib#376 on top of cslib#372.

  1. Eric suggested compiling these parametric monad programs to Prog for complexity.
  2. I thought we could generalise Prog.eval to Prog.liftM which would lift programs to arbitrary monads while we handle complexity through Prog.time. That way we can also probably reuse the mvcgen stuff

Maybe this message goes to a different thread.

Also imho TimeM is basically the additive version of writer monad (a distinction of additive/multiplicative writer monad that only arises in lean because of mathlib’s design decisions) . Both conceptually and organisationally it would make a lot of sense to rename it to AddWriter and move it to Foundations/Control/Monad.

This in turn makes an important part of cslib#376, just the monad transformer version of this AddWriter, say AddWriterT. We probably ought to create a folder for mtl style monad transformers (or maybe core needs to have all monad transformers?)

As it stands now, treating TimeM like it’s a separate concept is a bit anomalous w.r.t how we usually organise things. It does however make sense as an abbrev to AddWriter because of its specific use for algorithms.

It's unclear to me what #376 provides beyond what's already been demonstrated in #372. The mvcgen could be added to the free monad approach just as well, along with many other things Shreyas pruned from this PR for the sake of reviewability. And monad polymorphism doesn't avoid the gameability that comes with any monadic approach. The free monad has been used to formalize the algorithms we currently have in Cslib, and is able to reason about circuits, prove lower/upper bounds, formalize a web of reductions, generalize cost models, etc etc.

Like they mentioned above #376 can be built on top of #372 but currently it does not justify itself as an alternative, unless a case can be made at the level of models and reductions. I think Shreyas has provided sufficient argument in favor of this approach over the multiple months that the community has discussed and helped build it.

And like we've said before TimeM is really just a writer monad and I don't think it constitutes an "approach" to the problem at hand at all really.

I also wish to emphasise that I did initially treat cslib#275 initially as a research project to explore an idea of how to unify algorithms and complexity formalization that I have been talking about for two years (even before Geoffrey Irving’s announcement of the debate formalisation) namely the query+combinator approach (where thanks to @Tanner Duve the combinators just became monadic code because of his free monads). My source of this idea is the PiWare Agda library of Wouter Swierstra where they take a similar approach to synchronous circuits (combinators parametrised by a cell library.

At its current state cslib#372 is a distillation of the essentials and some basic examples alone that has been tuned into library code thanks to extremely rigorous reviews and later golfs by @Eric Wieser and then finally by @Chris Henson during their reviews. In addition to all th technical points above, I see none of this reflected in cslib#376, except it claims the word “query complexity” in its title, and the whole idea by implication.

So far I have an answer to 1 (@Shreyas Srinivas claims strictly more power, I'll wait for further opinions on this by @Kim Morrison and @Eric Wieser) and no answer to 2.

Just for everyone's info: I appreciate all the side-discussions, but these are so far only reiterating things already discussed and that I'm aware of, so I'm not engaging with them merely to keep this focused and speed up the process. I asked similar questions some time ago about power and ergonomics, but never got clear technical answer. Now there's enough code to formulate more precise arguments. These questions are important because there's little sense in having 3 approaches -- I suspect at least 2 of them would make good sense to be merged, but it's early to give a precise opinion.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

And Fabrizio : I think the extra annotation’s flexibility is important.

@Fabrizio Montesi : I have answered 2 here
That message and the one below.
Which translates to “yes you have to carry the model around after defining, but this is worth it and even necessary for the power and clarity it affords us”
Got it, so you're saying 1 and 2 are mutually exclusive. (This is important for justifying the presence of multiple approaches.)
Yes. It’s a small trade off for a big gain
I personally don’t see the need for multiple approaches since the ideas in cslib#376 can and should be built on top of cslib#372

And further I think the part where we (cslib#372) state our costs upfront should be required for algorithms theorists to even trust a formalisation (I am borrowing the words of one of our senior researchers in this community from Friday’s session)

Not much involved with any of the work here, but note that the parametric approach has a decisive advantage: it allows the verification of actual real-world Lean programs. No one in the real world uses free Monads because they lead to inefficient code. Expressivity-wise, I would expect both approaches to be equivalent, because you can express programs using free Monads using a final tagless encoding, which is effectively what the parametric approach does; you parameterize the program over the operations you want to measure (for example via type class) and then instantiate either with the timed model implementation or with the untimed real world (perhaps IO) implementation.

Whether we can use mvcgen to do cost proofs is independent of both approaches, I hope.
You can get that advantage in the free monad approach.
But more concretely I am trying to devise a framework for algorithms theory. Which is not always the same as real-world lean code.

The key difference in my approach is relevant here. I am explicitly stating what operations I count and how I count them, and I am therefore able to talk about, among other things, lower bounds, circuits, etc, and I am able to relate models to each other. Not only that, I can also talk about properties of custom query models independent of the algorithms I write with them.

And finally I am sure you would agree that we can turn Prog into ProgT and make it also work with any real lean code. So the explicit advantage you speak of can be built into this approach without losing the ability to properly formalize algorithms theory. This is what I mean when I insist that cslib#376 should be build atop my PR cslib#372. Thus it is not a clear advantage w.r.t. these two PRs.

So the "decisive" advantage you speak of is not really so w.r.t these two PRs.

In fact purely from a contribution guidelines perspective, cslib#376 should have

  1. First been discussed here on this Zulip, so that I am not expending my effort (several sleepless nights exploring multiple designs and then polishing what we have) for no reason on my PR (assuming cslib#376 did have this advantage, which I claim it doesn't).
  2. The contributor guidelines encourage working with what's available. Since this is possible and actually offers advantages, this is what ought to have happened.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

You can get that advantage in the free monad approach.

I'm very skeptical of that; it's far easier/reliable to specialize for type class instances than to specialize arbitrary other terms. I have had numerous discussions in the Haskell community about it.

I am explicitly stating what operations I count and how I count them, and I am therefore able to talk about, among other things, lower bounds, circuits, etc, and I am able to relate models to each other.

As long as there isn't a demonstrating example, I'm not convinced you couldn't do this with the other approach.

And finally I am sure you would agree that we can turn Prog into ProgT and make it also work with any real lean code.

Actually, I'm not deep enough into the topic to know what ProgT would look like and what it does. Furthermore, the fact that existing real-world code needs to be wrapped in ProgT (and linked to CSLib) just to verify resource bounds seems invasive to me. Relying on parametricity seems comparatively uninvasive.
The examples already existed and I have had to prune this PR

Shreyas Srinivas said:

The examples already existed and I have had to prune this PR

He's asking you to prove it can't be done in the parametric approach, not that it can be done in yours (that I believe).

Secondly the "verifying actual lean code" thing is part of pillar 2. This is explicitly in pillar 1. The goal of this PR is to build a framework to formalize the last 40 years of algorithmic theory, and our concern for implementability is very indirect. That is why the top down approach (start with custom models, reduce to RAM) even makes sense.

Fabrizio Montesi said:

Shreyas Srinivas said:

The examples already existed and I have had to prune this PR

He's asking you to prove it can't be done in the parametric approach, not that it can be done in yours (that I believe).

That's trying to prove a negative.
And finally, parametricity is completely orthogonal to what we are trying to accomplish here. To incorporate explicit reasoning about models.
I don't mind it if the FRO decides that they want a way to verify lean code, but then this ought to be a separate part of CSLib.
And lastly I object to the very title of the PR. It lays claim to an idea that it doesn't even use, and one that I have spent an awful lot of time and effort developing.

and lastly, I am not even sure you can generalize the theory of algorithmic complexity and reductions to code evaluated in arbitrary monads (even assuming you actually could state the queries explicitly). For example Cont monad can be used to introduce very non-trivial control flows. This is one reason I have stuck to evaluating in the Id monad. It's also just simpler.

And finally, you are not trying to set up mvcgen for arbitrary monads if you build on our approach. You only need to prove stuff in the Id monad which is where we evaluate a Prog right now. It's as if you took our Prog and just carried the annotations to the Id version of our program when we lift into Id and discarded them otherwise.
So the concern you express w.r.t this is not a blocker for using mvcgen. It might require tweaking to carry over annotations from Prog to Id into which it is lifted for evaluation.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

and lastly, I am not even sure you can generalize the theory of algorithmic complexity and reductions to code evaluated in arbitrary monads (even assuming you actually could state the queries explicitly). For example Cont monad can be used to introduce very non-trivial control flows. This is one reason I have stuck to evaluating in the Id monad. It's also just simpler.

I would consider your concern with verifying "real lean code", a decisive disadvantange as an algorithms theorist, even if I ignored the two obvious problems :

  1. not stating queries upfront. If you started doing this, then the PR ethically ought to build on top of mine, in terms of giving authorship and credit.

  2. The fact that it involves other monads which, from a correctness of algorithms perspective, we don't even care about, let alone understand well (source : I am actually doing my PhD with algorithms people and reviewing papers and everything in this community, albeit with a different research focus personally i.e. clocks, hardware, and such).

To summarise the discussion so far regarding my questions:

  1. cslib#372 looks like it has plenty of flexibility. I don't have a precise picture of cslib#376 in that regard yet, but I'd expect that reusing the same algorithm with different cost models is possible.
  2. I suspect this cannot be done in cslib#372. I'd like to know if it is possible in cslib#376.

What I see is that there are 3 approaches with distinctive merits so far and it appears to me at least 2 of them (TimeM + cslib#376 or cslib#372 + cslib#376) should probably be merged (depending on the answers to the above), possibly all 3 of them, in some order. But to figure out a direction I really need to understand the limitations and opportunities of cslib#376 better.

Note that I'm not talking about the technical implementations here, but rather the styles in which we write the algorithms. For example, if (2) is possible to do in cslib#376, then it probably subsumes the TimeM style currently in the repo.

Here's a concrete example of what might answer my question. Say I write:

def insertionSort [Monad m] [LE α] : List α → m (List α)

Can I now reason about insertionSort (α := Nat) under a custom-defined cost model for comparisons for nats? It seems likely, but maybe I'm not seeing something.

I think it is clear that both cslib#372 and cslib#376 subsume TimeM, so might I propose that the library could go for two options:

  1. cslib#372 + TimeM since it already works on top of TimeM (and we rename TimeM to AddWriter.
  2. cslib#376 + their choice of cslib#372 or TimeM. Or completely independent. Although here I do think they are defining an MTL-like transformer, so that they should probably rename to AddWriterT as TimeM should rename to AddWriter

( 1.) is my clear choice for algorithms theory, as an algorithms researcher.
For 2, I think the claims made in cslib#376 are a bit strong. @Eric Wieser said he'll clarify his thoughts on this so I'll wait for that. Modulo that it might be an alternative for verifying normal lean code where reasoning about relations between models is not a big concern (even though one could also do that in my framework).

Fabrizio Montesi said:

I have two questions:

  1. After squinting my eyes for a while, I could imagine ways to do almost anything interesting in both approach (reusing the same algorithm with different cost models, doing parametric complexity, proving lower bounds, etc.). Is that actually true?
  2. Real bliss in this case would be using a typeclass instead of an explicit parameter for the operations, for example:
public def insertionSort [Monad m] [LE α] : List α → m (List α)

Can that be done?

I'll let Shreyas and Kim have the final word/discussion here, but I'm not aware of any examples that are possible in one approach but aren't possible in the other, so the answer to (1) is probably Yes. What's more, lacking characteristic examples, the answer to (1) cannot be different to Yes.
(I think even my real-world algorithm expressivity argument can be refuted by simply copying the real-world algorithm into a model Prog variant that is defeq to the real-world algorithm for the appropriate instantiation. So cslib#372 just seems less convenient than cslib#376 in this regard, not less expressive.)

Regarding (2): I don't think either approach will give you [LE α], because both rely on an ambient monad to thread through the counter state (at the very least). There's no way a call to pure le : α -> α -> Prop can influence the ambient monad, hence such an operation couldn't be counted.
@Sebastian Graf : I think we should clarify what we mean by expressivity.
I think as far as lean programs go your statement about equivalence of expressivity is correct.

It’s just that by allowing this custom query type, I am allowing us to talk about other models of computation (including standard and custom ones that appear in the algorithms literature). Concretely I am saying that we talk about properties of models and reductions between them without even having to write algorithms. This is a separate layer of things my model makes trivial to express.

Also you don’t want [LE \alpha] in either approach because of this magic trick in lean called open Classical giving you free decidable instances for everything including LE even when you don’t declare it explicitly.

Sebastian Graf said:

Regarding (2): I don't think either approach will give you [LE α], because both rely on an ambient monad to thread through the counter state (at the very least). There's no way a call to pure le : α -> α -> Prop can influence the ambient monad, hence such an operation couldn't be counted.

Upon further reflection, I would go as far as saying: (2) "real bliss" is impossible to achieve at all, because the number of syntactic occurrences of a definition in an expression is not a semantic property. For example, in

def prog1 : Id Nat := do
let mut x := 0
for _ in [0:n] do
  if LE.le a b then x:=x+1 else x:=x+1
  foo
return x

is equivalent to

def prog2 : Id Nat := do
let mut x := 0
for _ in [0:n] do
  x:=x+1
  foo
return x

Clearly, we can prove prog1 = prog2. But the former has O(n) calls to LE.le, the latter O(1) (well, 0). So whether or not the program is in O(1) cannot be expressed in the logic (as a property p : Id Nat -> Prop, say, since otherwise we could prove false = p prog1 = p prog2 = true.

However, if (2) is a strong requirement (and I do think that UX is important), it may make sense to write a meta function that takes a (potentially pure) definition prog and a list of function calls to count (e.g., [`Le.le]), and then produces a new definition prog.counted (say) that wraps TimeM/TimeT around its result type and "instruments" calls to LE.le into TimeM, in the process replacing LE.le a b with some user-provided query function or something simple like do tick; pure (LE.le a b).
Concretely, for prog1 : Id Nat above, the meta function on [`LE.le] would instrument to (the elaborated Expr of)

def prog1.counted : TimeT Id Nat := do
let mut x := 0
for _ in [0:n] do
  if (<- tick; LE.le a b) then x:=x+1 else x:=x+1
  foo
return x

and this is no longer equivalent to the instrumentation of prog2, which is

def prog2.counted : TimeT Id Nat := do
let mut x := 0
for _ in [0:n] do
  x:=x+1
  foo
return x

and indeed one can find reasonable properties p : TimeT Id Nat -> Prop that differentiate prog1.counted from prog2.counted because they aren't equivalent; the property of whether or not the program has O(1) ticks is one such property. (Note that the meta function took the Expr syntax of prog1 and prog2 and made the function calls semantically observable.)

An attribute or custom elaborator (e.g., def prog1.counted := counting LE.le in prog1) could provide convenient syntax to use this meta function. I believe Sebastian U suggested writing an elaborator in a previous discussion.

So if (2) is really "I want to write regular Lean programs and post-hoc say what I want to count", then I say that is achievable, and independently so of the semantic encoding of "counting" (i.e. the present discussion). Although I'm no algorithms expert and maybe my idea of "counting" is too simplistic.

What you are suggesting with metaprogramming is close to what I implement with Prog . The difference is, I want to allow multiple layers of queries. I also want this “tick” size to depend on input size. When you start adding all this up, especially custom input dependent costs for queries, my systematic approach starts looking simpler and clearer.

Thanks for the detailed reasoning, @Sebastian Graf. Indeed I wanna know if we can offer at least one approach that offers good 'Lean ergonomics' (write a function as usual or almost and apply reasoning on costs later; supporting typeclasses as usual, like LE, is important here). One of the aims of CSLib is to build a substantial library of verified components, so this would be nice to have.

Writing a meta function was one of my first suggestions on the future plans for TimeM as well.
But Kim's parametric polymorphism approach forces the 'counting' already, so I was wondering if we could somehow instrument the typeclasses and their instances instead of the code of the algorithm.
Something like a lift operation that given LE returns LE in the Monad m.
Another intermediate-level solution could be to require people to define new typeclasses that mimic existing ones, like LECounted, I guess.

Re the different cost models and such, my informal thinking was that we could model different cost models simply by passing different monads to the algorithm, and these monads would be expressive enough to model even pretty complicated machinery. I'm sure this can be done in Shreyas' approach, but I'd appreciate some confirmation that it'd work also in Kim's approach.

Would you be able to reason inductively with this monadic typeclass? One of my approaches for circuits was inductive. Also, when you start building this currently hypothetical network of typeclasses to mimic my network of models, you are approaching the same ergonomics as my model. My model annotations get replaced by your MonadClass annotations
Notice that inside the code of the algorithm, we don’t have any annotations in my approach
The model annotations only show up in the complexity and correctness theorems.
The difference between this hypothetical network of monads and mine is that my models are still plain old inductive types.

In fact my algorithms have less annotation because you don’t even supply cmp as a function explicitly (and this is also where Eric pointed out other issues with cslib#376 to me). You just specify the query type and return type next to prog

The equivalent burden of specifying an inductive query type and cost model in cslib#376 is the listing of functions that my query types would have evaluated to (like their cmp) and potentially in future the cost functions. So where is this ergonomic advantage of cslib#376 exactly? It just moves the burden of work to a different place. And provides weaker reasoning.
And you lose all the niceness of inductive query types (their recursors, injectivity, pattern matching and all that). Afaik typeclasses can’t even be recursive.

What I am observing here @Fabrizio Montesi is that if the model of cslib#376 starts incorporating my features with typeclass network they suggest, their ergonomics approach mine, while (thanks to lack of recursive typeclasses), they still cannot model and reason about query types like I can. Also conceptually it starts looking more like our idea, (just excluding the authors of 372 from authorship ofc).

The current version of cslib#376 is far too primitive to make an apples to apples comparison of ergonomics ofc. The real comparison ofc would be when all the custom cost and model stuff is implemented.

Also @Fabrizio Montesi about LE an all that, core and mathlib versions of insertionSort and mergeSort use Bool predicates. A few commits prior to my most recent I also used LE. Eric showed me that there are multiple disadvantages to that.

Some of these observations are fair, and I'm investigating exactly because with cslib#372 I more or less know what I get, whereas with the old TimeM style and cslib#376 some thinking is required.
I don't get the comment about they cannot reason inductively in cslib#376, why?

Re LE: right, I see that their signature is

def List.mergeSort{α : Type u_1} (xs : List α) (le : α → α → Bool := by exact fun a b => a ≤ b) : List α

but using the default (important for ergonomics) means we're using an instance of LE anyway, doesn't it?
The issue remains: that parameter has type (le : α → α → Bool), instead of what's needed, e.g., (le : α → α → m Bool).

Mmmh... assuming the 'expressive' power in terms of reasoning is equivalent (to be established), and that ergonomics of function signatures and cheating-prevention are not so different (seems to be the case), are the following the key differences then? (I use separate numbers to distinguish from my original questions 1 and 2.)

  1. Using interpretation (FreeM) vs polymorphism.
  2. Collecting all operations under a single interface in the return type (cslib#372) vs taking the operations in one or multiple parameters of the function (cslib#376).

Also:

  1. Does 4 have important implications for the body of the function?

Fabrizio Montesi said:

I don't get the comment about they cannot reason inductively in cslib#376, why?

To be clear this is if they realize your informal idea of different typeclasses for different query models. Typeclasses can't have recursive fields (I believe structures could also not until fairly recently).

Re LE: right, I see that their signature is

def List.mergeSort{α : Type u_1} (xs : List α) (le : α → α → Bool := by exact fun a b => a ≤ b) : List α

but using the default (important for ergonomics) means we're using an instance of LE anyway, doesn't it?

You can, but sorting can be done on very general orders. I'll let Eric handle that.

The issue remains: that parameter has type (le : α → α → Bool), instead of what's needed, e.g., (le : α → α → m Bool).

only in cslib#376. In cslib#372 it is just (le : α → α → Bool). We are supplying it only when we model the query, not in the definition of the Prog itself.

The insertion sort Prog of cslib#372 is just :

def insertionSort (l : List α) : Prog (SortOpsInsertHead α) (List α) :=
  match l with
  | [] => return []
  | x :: xs => do
      let rest ← insertionSort xs
      insertOrd x rest

I don't think it is particular less ergonomic than cslib#376's 

public def insertionSort [Monad m] (cmp : α × α → m Bool) :
    List α → m (List α)
  | [] => pure []
  | x :: xs => do
    let sorted ← insertionSort cmp xs
    orderedInsert cmp x sorted
arguably it's more ergonomic
because I am not carrying this cmp around

Let's also compare cslib#376's ordered insertion function to mine
cslib#376:

public def orderedInsert [Monad m] (cmp : α × α → m Bool) (x : α) :
    List α → m (List α)
  | [] => pure [x]
  | y :: ys => do
    let lt ← cmp (x, y)
    if lt then
      pure (x :: y :: ys)
    else
      let rest ← orderedInsert cmp x ys
      pure (y :: rest)

cslib#372 :

def insertOrd (x : α) (l : List α) : Prog (SortOpsInsertHead α) (List α) := do
  match l with
  | [] => insertHead x l
  | a :: as =>
      if (← cmpLE x a : Bool) then
        insertHead x (a :: as)
      else
        let res ← insertOrd x as
        insertHead a res
They are practically the same. I have a slight overhead in the return type annotation and cslib#376 has to carry cmp around. For insertion sort, I even decided to count insertions for the heck of it.
If cslib#376 counted insertions, their type signature would get longer (with an insert function)

So I'd say that as queries get more complex (think RAM model), cslib#372 has better annotation ergonomics. Imagine adding 50 different function signatures to a RAM Model definition as you currently do for insertionSort in cslib#376. In cslib#372, you'd define one RAM query and one canonical cost function. This would be a big file, but beyond that, highly reusable

Update

Kim claimed that they had found an "exploit " in my FreeM model. This turned out to be a convenient choice in my model to use an le predicate in Prop with a Decidable instance instead of Bool, and absolutely nothing to do with using Free monads. it also had a typeclass parameter in the statement of the Prog, which is a dead give-away. No Prog program needs any instances. So it wasn’t an exploit in the first place.

Anyway, I switched my model to Bool to avoid the classical instances problem both models have
. One could easily craft a different typeclass that takes their monadic bool and produces a decidable prop (MonadDecidable?) and produce the same "exploit" in their model. The underlying point is, both models substantially cut down the scope for cheating. They eliminate it under current library code (meaning this can change) when models are carefully chosen. Human review is the only final guard. These models just reduce the surface area of exploitation.
I also laid out a plan to integrate their work on top of mine and retain its potential benefits as well as mine.

I quote below :

  1. Write a monad transformer version of TimeM (that's your TickT)
  2. Write a monad transformer version of FreeM.
  3. generalize Prog to ProgT.
  4. change queries and models to evaluate to this monadic type.

Basic definitions of complexity theory:

def UpperBound (f : α → Nat) (size : α → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop :=
  ∃ k, ∀ n x, size x ≤ n → f x <= k * bound n

def LowerBound (f : α → Nat) (size : α → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop :=
  ∃ k, ∀ n, ∃ x, size x ≤ n ∧ f x <= k * bound n

The TimeM, QueryTree and Prog "instrumentation monads" can wrap these uniformly — the wrappers are repetitive, suggesting a reusable meta-result is extractable. First QueryTree:

def QueryTree.UpperBound {α β γ δ : Type}
    (f : ∀ {m : Type → Type} [Monad m], (α → m β) → γ → m δ)
    (size : γ → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop :=
  Nat.UpperBound (α := (γ × (α → β)))
    (fun (x, oracle) => (f QueryTree.ask x : QueryTree α β δ).queriesOn oracle)
    (fun (x, _oracle) => size x)
    bound

def QueryTree.LowerBound {α β γ δ : Type}
    (f : ∀ {m : Type → Type} [Monad m], (α → m β) → γ → m δ)
    (size : γ → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop :=
  Nat.LowerBound (α := (γ × (α → β)))
    (fun (x, oracle) => (f QueryTree.ask x : QueryTree α β δ).queriesOn oracle)
    (fun (x, _oracle) => size x)
    bound

def Prog.UpperBound {α β : Type}
    (model : Model Q Nat)
    (prog : α → Prog Q β)
    (size : α → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop :=
  Nat.UpperBound
    (fun x => (prog x).cost model)
    (fun x => size x)
    bound

def Prog.LowerBound {α β : Type}
    (model : Model Q Nat)
    (prog : α → Prog Q β)
    (size : α → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop :=
  Nat.LowerBound
    (fun x => (prog x).cost model)
    (fun x => size x)
    bound

Note that Shreyas' framework puts an emphasis on one particular model (the cost of queries in particular), whereas Kim's framework emphasizes that the measured function f can't "cheat" by guessing the implementation of oracle, but in turn fixes the cost of each query to 1.

Now we combine both approaches. Below I pick Shreyas' Prog as the monad because it's more general than QueryTree. 

def Combined.UpperBound {α β : Type}
    (costModel : {ι : Type} → Q ι → Nat)
    (prog : α → Prog Q β)
    (size : α → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop :=
  Nat.UpperBound (α := (α × (∀ {ι}, Q ι → ι)))
    (fun (x, oracle) => (prog x : Prog Q β).cost (Model.mk oracle costModel))
    (fun (x, _oracle) => size x)
    bound

def Combined.LowerBound {α β : Type}
    (costModel : {ι : Type} → Q ι → Nat)
    (prog : α → Prog Q β)
    (size : α → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop :=
  Nat.LowerBound (α := (α × (∀ {ι}, Q ι → ι)))
    (fun (x, oracle) => (prog x : Prog Q β).cost (Model.mk oracle costModel))
    (fun (x, _oracle) => size x)
    bound

Note that because the oracle is passed only after prog has produced a "query plan", a sound implementation of prog has no way to cheat and "guess" what the oracle would respond. This is exactly the same guarantee that Kim's LowerBound definition gives. Interestingly, we no longer rely on parametricity here, which relieves us from the computable nuisance.
On the other hand, I think Shreyas can easily implement his complexity zoo on top of this abstraction, because the costModel is a parameter of the UpperBound proposition.

  | le (a b : α) : LEQuery α Bool

def Model.instLE (M : Model (LEQuery α) Cost) : LE α :=
  ⟨fun a b => M.evalQuery <| LEQuery.le a b⟩

structure IsSort
    (sort : List α → Prog (LEQuery α) (List α)) : Prop where
  /-- The sort produces a permutation of its input. -/
  perm : ∀ (xs : List α) (M : Model (LEQuery α) Cost), (sort xs).eval M |>.Perm xs
  /-- The sort produces a sorted list, for any totally ordered model. -/
  sorted : ∀ xs (M : Model (LEQuery α) Cost) [@Std.IsLinearOrder α M.instLE],
    (sort xs).eval M |>.Pairwise M.instLE.le
